KEY UPDATE, the bandit's deathbed confession: Muscatine News-Tribune 1904-10-25 p1 (image 543716346), "Dying Bandit Describes WHISKEY HOLLOW Hold-Up". This robbery IS the "Whiskey Hollow" hold-up (so it's 1904, not 1910). The gang leader, William Morris alias C.C. Blair, was mortally wounded by detectives in St. Louis and confessed to St. Louis police Chief Desmond. There were five men (one was "Collins", a Chicago tramp). They blew the express safe with nitroglycerin and got "nothing but a lot of cheap jewelry": "Watches, knives, forks and things", which they THREW AWAY "IN A CORN FIELD... about eight or ten miles south and three miles west of Columbus Junction". The paper also says they examined the loot "thirteen miles southwest of Columbus Junction". So a scatter of c.1904 express-shipment watches and cutlery in a field about 8-13 mi SSW of Columbus Junction (Louisa Co. IA, likely Morning Sun / Wapello / Oakville direction, depending on the engine route). A detector target if the field is identifiable. Whiskey Hollow, the hold-up spot: Muscatine News-Tribune 1904-09-14 p1 (image 543715370) says the leader boarded at Muscatine with a ticket to FRUITLAND, and "entering Whiskey Hollow, the train was laboring up grade" when he pulled the emergency brake at the robbers' bonfire on the right-of-way. So Whiskey Hollow is a grade on the Rock Island line south of Muscatine toward Fruitland (matching "7 mi S of Muscatine"). The gang had camped across the Mississippi beforehand (tent camp) and escaped downriver by skiff. Darkness and "dense woods" are noted there.

category: Native legend cache, NOT recovered, Michigan
place_as_named: Wabasis Lake, Oakfield/Grattan twp, Kent Co. MI (near Greenville and Belding); "supposed... within an arrow shot of the Wabasis club"; buried "near the base of a big black walnut tree or some other place"

In Sept 1904 Grand Rapids parties hired Elmer Cook to guide them to the lake "with instruments, charts and diagrams"
plss_placement: Wabasis Lake shore near the old Wabasis club site (today Wabasis Lake County Park, Kent Co.); secondary: Gardner farm S of Smyrna (killing site)
notes: For the MI thread. A well-known W. Michigan legend (Wabasis Lake Park has a historical marker about the chief). The newspaper source is good for a story pin. SECOND SOURCE: Belding Banner 1914-03-11 p1+p9 "...Surrounding Mystery: Supposed to Have Been Hidden by Old John Wabasis in the 40's" / p9 "Traditional Pot of Gold Left by Indians UNKNOWN" (https://www.newspapers.com/image/613579620/ , https://www.newspapers.com/image/613579692/): payment money for Flat River lands (Greenville to Lowell) hidden by Wabasis in an IRON BOX; band failed to find it; Wabasis killed and buried by the river bank; seances, D.P. Chapman & Son (Ionia gunsmiths) divining rod; GEORGE B. RACE's vision: clump of softwood trees on the NORTH BANK of LITTLE WABASIS lake, ground rising abruptly ~30 ft behind, a lone 6-inch tree on the rise, pot buried 4 ft at its base; Race and DR. P.C. COVILLE searched by boat ~a week driving rods - OUTCOME: they drove rods "in more than a thousand places", dug at every firm strike but found only stones; gave up after a week, "firm in the belief that the pot of money is still in the HILLSIDE that borders LITTLE WABASIS LAKE" (they thought the NE part of the box had rusted away, money heaped at the SE end). THIRD SOURCE 2026-10-31: Belding Banner 1922-02-15 p10 "...About Wabasis Gold" (https://www.newspapers.com/image/613603302/), a letter from F. G. STOCKING of San Jose CA, formerly of Belding, answering Judge Lapham's piece. He says the story came from the old chief's oldest daughter, who told his grandmother Stocking in "the old house on the farm north of town (where NORMAN OLSGAARD now lives)". The chief buried the money by their wigwam. When she told her sister, he got angry, dug it up, "put it in his canoe and went UP THE CREEK and no one ever knew where it was". It was "in a COPPER KETTLE and covered up with moss and was all in SILVER". Stocking dug for it as a boy at the camp site his father showed him, possibly on McFadden's land. He also knew "that Indian at KIDDVILLE" whose account agreed. Judge Lapham's piece (Belding Banner 1922-01-25 p8, https://www.newspapers.com/image/613603122/) is a humorous romance (Jimmy McFadden and Nancy Stocking on a farm bordering Wabasis Lake; a fake Alabama dowser letter), so treat it as folklore and not as evidence of a find. Net: silver in a copper kettle, moved by canoe up the creek (Wabasis Creek?) from the wigwam site; still unfound per the folklore. PLACEMENT 2026-10-31: Belding Banner 1914-04-01 p3, "Frank Stocking Writes Concerning John Wabasis Money" (letter from Morgan Hill CA, dated 16 Mar 1914; https://www.newspapers.com/image/613579965/). Chief JOHN WABASIS, sons Knockon and Boneyhim; the eldest daughter told grandmother Stocking. "Their CAMP was on the EAST SIDE of LITTLE WABASIS LAKE." The money "was all in silver... in a copper kettle, covered over with moss. The old chief took his canoe and went UP THROUGH THE LAKE and UP THE CREEK about 1-2 or 3-4 of a mile." "If any one ever finds that money they will find it close to the creek and less than a mile above the lake... LOOK ON THE SOUTH SIDE OF THE CREEK about 1-2 or 3-4 of a mile above the lake and about 10 RODS back from creek." Stocking also "hid a pick and shovel up there 35 years ago" (about 1879); their remains would mark the spot. So the target is the south bank of the inlet creek, 0.5-0.75 mi upstream of the lake and about 165 ft back. That conflicts with the 1914 Race/Coville hillside search at Little Wabasis. Which creek and which lake ("up through the lake") need a map check: Wabasis Creek above Wabasis Lake, Oakfield twp, Kent Co. Legend versions: Belding Banner 1921-12-21 p7 (Lakeview Enterprise reprint, "Lake Wabasis Once Haunted": Oakfield twp, Kent Co; the White Swan buried the treasure-gold "along the shores of the lake"; image 613604229). Grand Rapids Press 1932-08-06 p10 quotes the 1870 History and Directory of Kent County: Wabasee (White Swan) was exiled to "a small garden on the shore of Lake Wabasis" and killed at the Plainfield corn feast; his grave was "20 rods south of Plainfield bridge"; gold "supposed to be hidden on its shores" (image 1113034561).
